title: The Russian Military Beyond 2026 - Pain Points, Potential & Lessons for NATO (with Michael Kofman)
summary: Perun and Michael Kofman project the Russian military into 2027 and beyond: weakening infantry and air force, stabilised armour, a fast-growing drone and missile strike force, and economic and demographic limits after the war.

assertions.quote: Russia contracted for about 2,500 long-range one-way attack drones in 2023, 21,000 in 2024, 78,000 in 2025

verdicts.note: Open-source and Ukrainian intelligence estimates show Russian one-way attack drone output rising many-fold since 2023, with missile output also rising.
SIPRI says Russia's use of drones has expanded rapidly as it procures high volumes of cheaper systems, but it does not single out long-range strike drones or missiles.
DDIS reports long-range strikes rising sharply in 2025 with growing drone and missile production; its chart shows long-range drone output going from at least 500 in 2022 to at least 35,000 in 2025.

assertions.quote: the Russian Air Force 2026 was essentially a long way from closing some of its pre-war capability gaps.

verdicts.note: Analysts such as RUSI find Russian air power still weak at suppressing air defences and at complex air operations, relying on stand-off strikes.
US intelligence judges Russia's air and naval forces intact and arguably more capable than before the full-scale invasion.

assertions.quote: The Russian military does consistently show the ability to withstand high levels of attrition

verdicts.note: Despite very high casualties since 2022, Russia has kept recruiting and expanded its force while sustaining offensive operations.
DDIS judges Russia better positioned than Ukraine for a war of attrition thanks to ongoing recruitment and greater production capacity.
US intelligence says Russia's ground forces have grown even with wartime attrition and Moscow is confident it will prevail.
UCDP: confirmed Russian combat deaths grew each year to 77,700 in 2025 while the war stayed the world's deadliest for a third year, showing that Russia has kept fighting through heavy losses so far.

assertions.quote: staying north of 7% of GDP probably just isn't going to be realistic longer term

verdicts.note: Deficits, rising debt and deferred civilian spending strain the budget, but states have sustained high military spending for years when they accept the trade-offs.

Russian spending growth slowed to 5.9 percent in 2025, the slowest since 2022, while defence hit a record 20 percent of government spending and social costs mounted, yet Russia has so far kept raising it despite sanctions.

DDIS finds military spending is squeezing other sectors, reserves are limited and growth has stalled, with sharper inflation and shortages ahead, but the regime will keep prioritising the war and its build-up.
EFIS: Russia's economy has entered a downturn with defence growing at civilian expense, but a complete collapse remains highly unlikely.

assertions.quote: unless the Russians find a way to make up the numbers quickly, the active duty force will have to shrink.

verdicts.note: Many contracts are held only by stop-loss and the force is old, but Moscow could raise conscription or pay to hold numbers.

assertions.quote: tactical level exercises between NATO militaries and Ukrainian militaries show that we have a problem there.

verdicts.note: Exercise reports and munitions-stock shortfalls point to gaps in counter-drone defence and mass missile defence, though NATO is adapting.

assertions.quote: European NATO military spending has surged and that trend is likely to continue at least into the medium term

verdicts.note: SIPRI and NATO figures show European military spending rising sharply each year since 2022, with a 5% of GDP pledge agreed in 2025.
European NATO countries have committed to new spending targets, Poland already meets them and Germany has a half-trillion-euro defence surge.
European spending rose 14 percent in 2025 to a record $864 billion and doubled over 2016-25; the 29 European NATO members spent $559 billion.
US intelligence says European leaders are reversing decades of underinvestment, raising defence spending and pledging dramatically higher commitments.

assertions.quote: is for Russia to actually struggle to keep up in the defense industrial competition in the longer term.

verdicts.note: Europe's economy is many times Russia's, but turning money into forces is slow and Russia's war industry is already running.
DDIS expects Russia to out-produce Europe in the coming years, while noting labour shortages, debt and an economy under strain that make further growth beyond 2025 hard; the long run is left open.
